## Certification and compliance records (44)

### FCC equipment authorization (FCC)
- Page: https://hi-spark.net/certification/fcc.html
- Group: Radio and telecom | Region: United States | Status: Mandatory for radio products
- Issued or recognised by: Federal Communications Commission (FCC)
- Summary: U.S. equipment authorization rules for radio transmitters, intentional radiators and certain electronic products placed on the American market.
- Meaning: Any device that transmits radio energy in the United States normally needs an FCC authorization before it can be marketed or imported. Devices fall into Certification, Supplier’s Declaration of Conformity or verification routes depending on the radio technology.
- Applies to: Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, cellular and sub-GHz radios; Unintentional radiators such as switching electronics; Wireless modules and host devices that contain them
- Does not cover: Electrical safety, which is handled by NRTL listing such as UL or ETL; RF exposure to users unless the device is assessed against the exposure limits; Cybersecurity or privacy of the device or its cloud
- Verification checklist: Identify the correct authorization route for each radio; Test to the applicable FCC rule part at an accredited lab; Keep the FCC ID label and user manual statements accurate; Complete the supplier’s declaration or certification filing; List the module grant conditions when using a pre-certified module
- Sources: FCC Equipment Authorization https://www.fcc.gov/engineering-technology/laboratory-division/equipment-authorization; FCC rules (47 CFR Part 15) https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-47/chapter-I/subchapter-A/part-15
- Last verified: 2026-10-10

### ISED radio certification (Canada) (ISED)
- Page: https://hi-spark.net/certification/ised.html
- Group: Radio and telecom | Region: Canada | Status: Mandatory for radio products
- Issued or recognised by: Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada
- Summary: Canadian radio equipment certification and labelling rules, managed under the spectrum management programme of ISED.
- Meaning: Wireless products sold in Canada require an ISED certification number and the correct label wording, usually in both English and French. Test reports from an accredited lab are accepted through a recognised certification body.
- Applies to: Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and cellular devices; Sub-GHz remote controls and sensors; Wireless modules imported into Canada
- Does not cover: Canadian electrical safety approval (cUL or equivalent); Provincial consumer protection requirements; Cybersecurity obligations
- Verification checklist: Select the correct RSS standard for the radio; Test and obtain a certification number from a recognised body; Apply the ISED label and bilingual user statements; Record the hardware and firmware version tested
- Sources: ISED spectrum management https://ised-isde.canada.ca/site/spectrum-management-telecommunications/en
- Last verified: 2026-10-10

### CE marking under the Radio Equipment Directive (CE / RED)
- Page: https://hi-spark.net/certification/ce.html
- Group: Radio and telecom | Region: European Union | Status: Mandatory in the EU
- Issued or recognised by: Notified bodies and the manufacturer under EU law
- Summary: The Radio Equipment Directive 2014/53/EU is the main route to CE marking for wireless products sold in the European Union.
- Meaning: Manufacturers declare conformity, apply the CE mark and produce a technical file. From 1 August 2025 the delegated regulation on cybersecurity for internet-connected radio equipment adds mandatory security requirements.
- Applies to: Any product containing a radio transmitter; Devices that combine radio, GPS or cellular functions; Internet-connected radio equipment, including apps that control them
- Does not cover: A CE mark alone does not prove a product is secure or future-proof; Chemical or packaging obligations handled by RoHS, REACH and packaging rules; National spectrum restrictions that still apply inside the EU
- Verification checklist: Identify the applicable directives and harmonised standards; Decide whether a notified body is required; Build and retain the technical file for the required period; Sign the EU declaration of conformity; Apply the CE mark, importer details and language requirements
- Sources: EU Radio Equipment Directive https://single-market-economy.ec.europa.eu/sectors/electrical-and-electronic-engineering-industries-eei/radio-equipment-directive-red_en; EUR-Lex delegated regulation 2022/30 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg_del/2022/30/oj
- Last verified: 2026-10-10

### UKCA marking (Great Britain) (UKCA)
- Page: https://hi-spark.net/certification/ukca.html
- Group: Radio and telecom | Region: United Kingdom | Status: Mandatory in Great Britain
- Issued or recognised by: UK approved bodies and the manufacturer
- Summary: The UK conformity assessment marking used for most products placed on the market in Great Britain, with separate rules in Northern Ireland.
- Meaning: UKCA marking mirrors much of the EU framework after Brexit. The UK government has continued to recognise CE marking for most goods, but radio equipment, security products and labelling rules should be checked per product before shipping.
- Applies to: Radio equipment placed on the Great Britain market; Products where the manufacturer chooses the UKCA route; Importers and distributors holding stock in the UK
- Does not cover: Northern Ireland, where specific UKNI arrangements apply; EU market access, which still needs CE marking; Product-specific approvals such as gas or medical devices
- Verification checklist: Confirm whether CE or UKCA is the accepted route for your product; Use a UK approved body where third-party assessment is required; Keep the UK declaration of conformity with UK responsible person details; Apply the UKCA mark and correct labelling
- Sources: Using the UKCA marking https://www.gov.uk/guidance/using-the-ukca-marking
- Last verified: 2026-10-10

### Brazilian telecommunications homologation (Anatel)
- Page: https://hi-spark.net/certification/anatel.html
- Group: Radio and telecom | Region: Brazil | Status: Mandatory for telecom products
- Issued or recognised by: Agência Nacional de Telecomunicações (Anatel)
- Summary: Homologation required before telecom and radio products may be sold or connected to Brazilian networks.
- Meaning: Anatel homologation is granted to a local representative, and the approved model is published with a homologation number that must appear on the product or in the manual.
- Applies to: Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, cellular and RF products; Cables, connectors and network equipment; Devices that connect to public telecom networks
- Does not cover: INMETRO safety certification where the product also falls under that scope; Consumer warranty and after-sales law obligations; Tax and import registration
- Verification checklist: Appoint a Brazilian representative as a legal holder; Test at an accredited lab against the applicable Anatel acts; Register the product and obtain the homologation number; Display the number and keep the certificate current
- Sources: Anatel https://www.gov.br/anatel/pt-br
- Last verified: 2026-10-10

### Mexican telecommunications approval (IFT)
- Page: https://hi-spark.net/certification/ift.html
- Group: Radio and telecom | Region: Mexico | Status: Mandatory for telecom products
- Issued or recognised by: Instituto Federal de Telecomunicaciones (IFT)
- Summary: Mexican homologation for products that use the radio spectrum or connect to public telecom networks.
- Meaning: Approval is issued through a Mexican holder and results in a homologation certificate that must be referenced in labelling and documentation for the Mexican market.
- Applies to: Mobile phones, tablets, wearables and Wi-Fi devices; Radio modules and network equipment; Voice and data terminal equipment
- Does not cover: NOM safety and efficiency rules that may also apply; Customs clearance procedures; Software services operated from outside Mexico
- Verification checklist: Confirm whether the product is homologable or exempt; Appoint the Mexican holder and file the application; Test against IFT technical provisions; Label the product with the homologation reference
- Sources: IFT https://www.ift.org.mx/
- Last verified: 2026-10-10

### KC certification (South Korea) (KC)
- Page: https://hi-spark.net/certification/kc.html
- Group: Radio and telecom | Region: South Korea | Status: Mandatory for radio products
- Issued or recognised by: National Radio Research Agency (RRA) under MSIT
- Summary: Korean certification for radio equipment, combining radio conformity and, in many cases, electrical safety and EMC approval.
- Meaning: KC certification uses different routes: conformity certification, registration or a supplier declaration, depending on the radio type and power. Certificates are held by a Korean representative.
- Applies to: Wi-Fi and Bluetooth products; Cellular and IoT modules; Broadcast receivers and RF equipment
- Does not cover: Korean e-waste and recycling registration, which is separate; Content or service regulation; Cybersecurity requirements
- Verification checklist: Classify the equipment and choose the right KC route; Test to Korean technical standards; Appoint a Korean representative to hold the certificate; Apply the KC mark and Korean-language label statements
- Sources: National Radio Research Agency (RRA) https://www.rra.go.kr/en/index.do
- Last verified: 2026-10-10

### Japanese radio certification (Giteki) (MIC / TELEC)
- Page: https://hi-spark.net/certification/mic-telec.html
- Group: Radio and telecom | Region: Japan | Status: Mandatory for radio products
- Issued or recognised by: Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications (MIC) through registered bodies
- Summary: Japanese technical conformity certification for radio equipment, commonly known as the Giteki mark and administered through registered certification bodies.
- Meaning: Radio equipment must be certified and carry the Giteki mark with the certification number. Products that include a certified module may still need their own certification if the module conditions are not met.
- Applies to: Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, RFID and cellular devices; Wireless modules and antennas; Short-range remote controls
- Does not cover: Japanese electrical safety obligations such as PSE for certain power supplies; Telecom network connection approval beyond the radio function; Cybersecurity regulation
- Verification checklist: Determine whether the module certification can be reused; Apply to a registered Japanese certification body; Label the Giteki mark and certification number; Keep the construction-protection documentation current
- Sources: MIC technical regulations https://www.tele.soumu.go.jp/e/
- Last verified: 2026-10-10

### Taiwan NCC type approval (NCC)
- Page: https://hi-spark.net/certification/ncc-tw.html
- Group: Radio and telecom | Region: Taiwan | Status: Mandatory for radio products
- Issued or recognised by: National Communications Commission (NCC)
- Summary: Taiwanese type approval for low-power radio equipment and telecom terminal devices sold on the local market.
- Meaning: Approved products receive a NCC certification number and must carry the NCC mark. The application is normally filed by a Taiwanese representative company.
- Applies to: Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and RF products; Mobile and wearable devices with radios; Telecom terminal equipment
- Does not cover: Taiwan BSMI electrical safety and EMC certification, which is separate; Battery transport and recycling schemes; Software service compliance
- Verification checklist: Confirm whether approval is required for the radio band and power; Test at a recognised Taiwanese laboratory; File through a local agent; Apply the NCC mark and label content in Traditional Chinese
- Sources: Taiwan NCC https://www.ncc.gov.tw/english/
- Last verified: 2026-10-10

### Australian and New Zealand RCM (RCM)
- Page: https://hi-spark.net/certification/rcm.html
- Group: Radio and telecom | Region: Australia and New Zealand | Status: Mandatory for radio and mains products
- Issued or recognised by: ACMA and the EESS regulators
- Summary: The Regulatory Compliance Mark shows that a product meets Australian and New Zealand radio communications and, where applicable, electrical safety requirements.
- Meaning: The supplier must be registered in the national database and hold test evidence for radio, EMC and safety requirements. Labelling rules differ between radio and electrical safety scopes.
- Applies to: Radio communications devices; Mains-powered electrical products; Devices that combine both scopes
- Does not cover: Telecommunications cabling or carrier connection approval; Battery recycling obligations; Voluntary efficiency ratings
- Verification checklist: Identify whether radio, EESS or both schemes apply; Register as a responsible supplier; Hold compliant test reports with the required standards; Apply the RCM with the correct size and placement
- Sources: ACMA compliance https://www.acma.gov.au/radiocommunications-licences; EESS https://www.eess.gov.au/
- Last verified: 2026-10-10

### Saudi SASO conformity (SASO)
- Page: https://hi-spark.net/certification/saso.html
- Group: Radio and telecom | Region: Saudi Arabia | Status: Mandatory in Saudi Arabia
- Issued or recognised by: Saudi Standards, Metrology and Quality Organization
- Summary: Product conformity used for goods entering Saudi Arabia, issued through the SABER platform with certificate of conformity procedures.
- Meaning: Importers must register the product and obtain the required certificates of conformity before customs clearance. Radio and telecom products also need CITC approval.
- Applies to: Electrical and electronic consumer products; Radio and telecom devices; Products in regulated technical regulations
- Does not cover: CITC radio and telecom licensing, which is handled separately; Halal or food-related schemes; Commercial agency registration
- Verification checklist: Confirm the technical regulation that applies to the product; Register the product in SABER and select the conformity route; Test to the applicable Saudi standard or approved equivalent; Attach the certificate to each shipment
- Sources: SASO https://www.saso.gov.sa/en/Pages/default.aspx
- Last verified: 2026-10-10

### Eurasian EAC conformity (EAC)
- Page: https://hi-spark.net/certification/eac.html
- Group: Radio and telecom | Region: Eurasia Economic Union | Status: Mandatory in EAEU markets
- Issued or recognised by: National accreditation bodies of the EAEU member states
- Summary: EAC conformity for products placed on the Eurasian Economic Union market, covering safety, EMC and, for some categories, radio requirements.
- Meaning: Products assessed against the relevant technical regulations, for example low-voltage, EMC and EMC-of-radio rules, receive an EAC declaration or certificate that is valid across the member states.
- Applies to: Electrical and electronic products; Radio and low-voltage equipment; Machinery and household appliances
- Does not cover: Local telecom operator licensing; Voluntary export schemes; Language requirements outside the technical regulations
- Verification checklist: Map the product against the applicable TR CU regulations; Decide between declaration and certification routes; Use an accredited body in a member state; Mark the product with the EAC mark and Cyrillic information where required
- Sources: Eurasian Economic Union https://eec.eaeunion.org/en/
- Last verified: 2026-10-10

### Indian BIS registration and WPC approval (BIS / WPC)
- Page: https://hi-spark.net/certification/bis-wpc.html
- Group: Radio and telecom | Region: India | Status: Mandatory for regulated products
- Issued or recognised by: Bureau of Indian Standards and the Wireless Planning and Coordination wing
- Summary: Indian compliance typically combines BIS registration for electronics safety under the CRS scheme with WPC approval for wireless products.
- Meaning: BIS registration is issued to the manufacturer through the Compulsory Registration Scheme, while the WPC equipment type approval covers the radio interface. Both can be needed for one product.
- Applies to: Electronics covered by the CRS list; Wi-Fi and Bluetooth devices; Telecom and RF equipment
- Does not cover: Indian telecom network licensing; Local manufacturing incentives; Consumer packaging declarations outside the schemes
- Verification checklist: Check whether the product appears in the CRS schedule; Test in a BIS-recognised laboratory; Apply for WPC ETA for the radio module; Apply the standard mark once registration is granted
- Sources: Bureau of Indian Standards https://www.bis.gov.in/; WPC https://www.wpc.dot.gov.in/
- Last verified: 2026-10-10

### China SRRC and CCC approval (SRRC / CCC)
- Page: https://hi-spark.net/certification/srrc-ccc.html
- Group: Radio and telecom | Region: China | Status: Mandatory in China
- Issued or recognised by: MIIT, SRRC and CNCA-designated bodies
- Summary: Wireless products entering China normally require SRRC radio type approval, with CCC compulsory certification for categories on the CCC list.
- Meaning: SRRC approval covers the radio transmitter type, and CCC covers safety and EMC for products in scope. Both are held by a local entity and are checked at import and sale.
- Applies to: Radio transmitting equipment; Products in the CCC catalogue, including some IT and AV equipment; Wireless modules and finished devices
- Does not cover: China RoHS packaging disclosure, which is a separate obligation; Cybersecurity review for critical network equipment; Software service licensing
- Verification checklist: Determine SRRC scope and the radio test standard; Check whether the product is in the CCC catalogue; Appoint a local applicant and submit samples; Apply the SRRC code and CCC mark as required
- Sources: MIIT https://www.miit.gov.cn/; CNCA https://www.cnca.gov.cn/
- Last verified: 2026-10-10

### North American safety listing (UL / ETL)
- Page: https://hi-spark.net/certification/ul-etl.html
- Group: Safety and EMC | Region: United States and Canada | Status: Required by retailers and inspectors
- Issued or recognised by: UL, Intertek (ETL), CSA and other NRTLs
- Summary: Third-party product safety certification for the North American market, issued by a Nationally Recognized Testing Laboratory.
- Meaning: Safety listing is not a single government mark: it is a certification issued by an NRTL against UL or CSA standards. Retailers, insurers and electrical inspectors commonly require it, and the mark must match the exact product and factory.
- Applies to: Mains-powered IoT devices, hubs and chargers; Battery-powered products with charging circuits; Components such as power supplies inside a device
- Does not cover: Radio approval, which is the FCC or ISED scope; Performance, privacy or cybersecurity of the product; Software updates that change the safety-relevant design
- Verification checklist: Identify the correct UL or CSA standard for the product; Submit samples and critical components to the NRTL; Accept the factory inspection programme for listed products; Report design changes that affect safety before shipping them
- Sources: UL certification https://www.ul.com/services/certification; CSA Group testing and certification https://www.csagroup.org/testing-certification/
- Last verified: 2026-10-10

### IEC and EN 62368-1 safety standard (IEC 62368-1)
- Page: https://hi-spark.net/certification/iec-62368.html
- Group: Safety and EMC | Region: International | Status: Core safety standard
- Issued or recognised by: International Electrotechnical Commission
- Summary: The hazard-based safety standard that replaced IEC 60950 and IEC 60065 for audio, video, information and communication technology equipment.
- Meaning: Rather than prescribing construction, IEC 62368-1 requires the designer to identify energy sources and provide safeguards. It is the safety standard that most smart speakers, hubs, cameras and chargers are tested against.
- Applies to: Audio and video equipment; IT and communication equipment; Devices with mains or battery power and a charging interface
- Does not cover: Radio approval; Medical or automotive safety standards; Cybersecurity of the device or cloud
- Verification checklist: Classify energy sources and required safeguards; Check component ratings and creepage and clearance distances; Test abnormal and single-fault conditions; Review the standard edition used in each market certificate
- Sources: IEC https://www.iec.ch/
- Last verified: 2026-10-10

### EMC Directive 2014/30/EU (EMC)
- Page: https://hi-spark.net/certification/emc-directive.html
- Group: Safety and EMC | Region: European Union | Status: Mandatory in the EU
- Issued or recognised by: Manufacturer under EU law, with notified bodies where required
- Summary: The European directive that requires equipment to limit electromagnetic emissions and to be immune to interference in its intended environment.
- Meaning: EMC is assessed separately from radio and safety. Products that contain radios are usually covered by the Radio Equipment Directive, which combines radio and EMC requirements in one file.
- Applies to: Electrical and electronic equipment with possible emissions; Devices with switching power supplies or motors; Equipment intended for residential, commercial or industrial environments
- Does not cover: Radio spectrum authorisation; Electrical safety; Immunity performance guarantees in every real installation
- Verification checklist: Identify whether RED or EMC Directive applies; Test emissions and immunity against harmonised standards; Document the assessment and any applicable standards; Include EMC statements in the declaration and manual
- Sources: EU EMC Directive https://single-market-economy.ec.europa.eu/sectors/electrical-and-electronic-engineering-industries-eei/electromagnetic-compatibility-emc-directive_en
- Last verified: 2026-10-10

### IECEE CB Scheme certificate (CB Scheme)
- Page: https://hi-spark.net/certification/cb-scheme.html
- Group: Safety and EMC | Region: International | Status: Voluntary, widely used
- Issued or recognised by: IECEE member certification bodies
- Summary: An international system that lets one safety test report and certificate be converted into national certifications in participating countries.
- Meaning: The CB Scheme reduces repeated safety testing across countries. A CB test certificate and report from one member body is accepted as the basis for national approval by other members, sometimes with national differences added.
- Applies to: Products needing safety approval in several countries; Power supplies, chargers and appliances; Components with their own standards
- Does not cover: Radio approvals, which are handled by national telecom schemes; Marking requirements, which stay national; Factory inspection regimes of individual schemes
- Verification checklist: Choose a CB test laboratory recognised in the target countries; Confirm national differences before testing; Request the CB certificate and full test report; Convert the report into national certificates where needed
- Sources: IECEE CB Scheme https://www.iecee.org/cb-scheme
- Last verified: 2026-10-10

### IEC 60529 IP rating (IP)
- Page: https://hi-spark.net/certification/ip-rating.html
- Group: Safety and EMC | Region: International | Status: Voluntary, widely demanded
- Issued or recognised by: Testing laboratories against IEC 60529
- Summary: Ingress protection rating that describes resistance to dust and water, written as IP followed by two digits.
- Meaning: The first digit covers solids and dust, the second covers water. Ratings apply to the complete enclosure as tested, not to the electronics inside, and can be voided if the housing is opened or seals are reused.
- Applies to: Outdoor cameras and doorbells; Sensors exposed to humidity or rain; Portable devices with sealing requirements
- Does not cover: Impact resistance, which is covered by IK ratings; Corrosion resistance and salt spray; Continued protection after repair or battery replacement
- Verification checklist: Select the rating required by the installation environment; Test the finished product, including seals and gaskets; Include cable glands and connectors in the assessment; State the test conditions in marketing material
- Sources: IEC IP ratings https://www.iec.ch/ip-ratings
- Last verified: 2026-10-10

### CSA Group certification (CSA)
- Page: https://hi-spark.net/certification/csa.html
- Group: Safety and EMC | Region: Canada and United States | Status: Common market requirement
- Issued or recognised by: CSA Group
- Summary: Canadian safety certification that is also accepted as an NRTL listing for the United States market.
- Meaning: CSA marks show that a product has been evaluated against Canadian and, where applicable, U.S. standards. This is often the most practical route for products sold in both countries at once.
- Applies to: Electrical and electronic products for Canada; Products seeking a combined Canada and U.S. listing; Components that require certified parts
- Does not cover: Radio equipment certification in either country; Provincial electrical code requirements; Cybersecurity and privacy
- Verification checklist: Confirm which CSA or UL standards apply in each country; Choose a combined Canada and U.S. certification if possible; Keep the factory inspection programme current; Report changes to critical components
- Sources: CSA Group https://www.csagroup.org/testing-certification/
- Last verified: 2026-10-10

### Restriction of Hazardous Substances (RoHS)
- Page: https://hi-spark.net/certification/rohs.html
- Group: Environmental and materials | Region: European Union and aligned markets | Status: Mandatory in scope
- Issued or recognised by: Manufacturer declaration under EU Directive 2011/65/EU
- Summary: Restricts lead, mercury, cadmium, hexavalent chromium and certain phthalates in electrical and electronic equipment sold in the EU.
- Meaning: RoHS compliance is shown through a technical file, supplier declarations and material test reports rather than a product mark. Many other markets have adopted similar restrictions, sometimes with different substance lists.
- Applies to: Electrical and electronic equipment in the ten RoHS categories; Components and sub-assemblies placed on the market; Cables, power supplies and accessories sold with the device
- Does not cover: Batteries, which have their own regulation; Packaging, which is covered by packaging rules; Product safety or radio performance
- Verification checklist: Collect supplier declarations and material test reports; Assess homogeneous material levels rather than the finished product; Keep evidence for every part number in the bill of materials; Refresh evidence when a supplier changes a material or process
- Sources: EU RoHS Directive https://environment.ec.europa.eu/topics/waste-and-recycling/rohs-directive_en
- Last verified: 2026-10-10

### REACH SVHC and SCIP notification (REACH)
- Page: https://hi-spark.net/certification/reach.html
- Group: Environmental and materials | Region: European Union | Status: Mandatory in scope
- Issued or recognised by: European Chemicals Agency framework
- Summary: European chemicals regulation that places duties on suppliers when a product contains a Substance of Very High Concern above the threshold.
- Meaning: IoT hardware can contain SVHCs in solder, plastics, coatings or cables. Information duties apply at the article level, and SCIP database notification is required for articles placed on the EU market.
- Applies to: Finished articles placed on the EU market; Components imported as separate articles; Cables, housings and coatings
- Does not cover: Restriction of hazardous substances in electronics, which is RoHS; Battery chemical restrictions; Occupational exposure rules inside factories
- Verification checklist: Collect full material declarations from suppliers; Check the current SVHC candidate list regularly; Communicate information down the supply chain when required; Prepare SCIP notifications for the affected articles
- Sources: ECHA REACH https://echa.europa.eu/regulations/reach/understanding-reach
- Last verified: 2026-10-10

### Waste Electrical and Electronic Equipment (WEEE)
- Page: https://hi-spark.net/certification/weee.html
- Group: Environmental and materials | Region: European Union and United Kingdom | Status: Mandatory in scope
- Issued or recognised by: National producer responsibility schemes
- Summary: Rules that make producers responsible for financing the collection and recycling of electrical and electronic equipment.
- Meaning: Sellers that place products on the market usually have to register with a national producer responsibility organisation in each country, report volumes and display the crossed-out bin symbol.
- Applies to: Household and professional electrical equipment; Online sellers, including distance sellers into the EU; Batteries contained in the product
- Does not cover: RoHS substance restrictions; Packaging recovery schemes; Transport and logistics obligations
- Verification checklist: Register in every EU country where you place goods; Report put-on-market volumes on time; Print the crossed-out bin symbol and producer identification; Contract with a take-back scheme where required
- Sources: EU WEEE Directive https://environment.ec.europa.eu/topics/waste-and-recycling/waste-electrical-and-electronic-equipment-weee_en
- Last verified: 2026-10-10

### EU Battery Regulation (EU) 2023/1542 (EU Battery)
- Page: https://hi-spark.net/certification/eu-battery.html
- Group: Environmental and materials | Region: European Union | Status: Mandatory, phased
- Issued or recognised by: EU member state authorities
- Summary: Replaces the older battery directive with wider duties covering carbon footprint, recycled content, labelling, due diligence and removability.
- Meaning: The regulation applies progressively, so different obligations start on different dates. Portable batteries designed into IoT products face removability and replaceability expectations, and labelling requirements expand over time.
- Applies to: Products with rechargeable or replaceable batteries; Battery pack suppliers; Producers placing batteries on the EU market
- Does not cover: Transport testing of lithium cells, which is UN 38.3; Safety testing of the battery pack; Recycling targets handled by national schemes
- Verification checklist: Identify the battery category and the applicable phase-in dates; Plan for removability and replaceability of portable batteries; Prepare carbon footprint and recycled content documentation; Apply the battery labelling and QR requirements when they apply
- Sources: EU batteries policy https://environment.ec.europa.eu/topics/waste-and-recycling/batteries_en
- Last verified: 2026-10-10

### California Proposition 65 (Prop 65)
- Page: https://hi-spark.net/certification/prop65.html
- Group: Environmental and materials | Region: California, United States | Status: Mandatory if exposure triggers
- Issued or recognised by: California Office of Environmental Health Hazard Assessment
- Summary: California law that requires a clear warning when a product exposes users to chemicals on the state list above safe harbour levels.
- Meaning: The rule is warning-based rather than approval-based. Manufacturers either assess exposure and warn, or document that exposure is below the safe harbour level. Warning content and placement follow set formats.
- Applies to: Consumer products sold in California; Cables, vinyl materials, solder and coatings; Products where a chemical may be released during normal use
- Does not cover: Federal chemical restrictions; EU substance rules; Product safety certification
- Verification checklist: Screen the bill of materials against the current chemical list; Assess likely exposure routes and duration of use; Choose between a warning and a documented no-exposure case; Apply the warning in the required format and refresh the review
- Sources: California OEHHA https://oehha.ca.gov/proposition-65
- Last verified: 2026-10-10

### UN 38.3 lithium battery transport testing (UN 38.3)
- Page: https://hi-spark.net/certification/un383.html
- Group: Environmental and materials | Region: International transport | Status: Mandatory for shipping
- Issued or recognised by: UN Manual of Tests and Criteria, tested by accredited labs
- Summary: Transport test requirement for lithium metal and lithium ion cells and batteries before air, sea or land shipment.
- Meaning: Shipping lithium batteries without a UN 38.3 test summary is a transport regulation violation, and carriers can refuse the shipment. The test report accompanies the battery through the supply chain, including sample shipments.
- Applies to: Devices with lithium ion or lithium metal cells; Replacement battery packs; Prototype and sample shipments
- Does not cover: Battery safety certification of the finished product; Charging system design; Consumer warnings beyond transport labelling
- Verification checklist: Test each cell and battery type as shipped; Hold the test summary from an accredited laboratory; Check state of charge and packaging rules for air transport; Re-test after design or supplier changes that affect the battery
- Sources: UN transport of dangerous goods https://unece.org/transport/standards/transport/dangerous-goods
- Last verified: 2026-10-10

### Energy Star efficiency programme (Energy Star)
- Page: https://hi-spark.net/certification/energy-star.html
- Group: Environmental and materials | Region: United States and selected markets | Status: Voluntary
- Issued or recognised by: US Environmental Protection Agency
- Summary: Voluntary efficiency labelling for products that meet Energy Star specifications in an eligible category.
- Meaning: For network equipment and consumer electronics, Energy Star certification requires third-party testing and registration, and the label must be used only for the certified configuration.
- Applies to: Eligible consumer electronics and network equipment; Products where efficiency is a selling point; Retail programmes that require the label
- Does not cover: Safety, EMC or radio approval; EU energy labelling, which is a separate scheme; Inverter or motor efficiency standards
- Verification checklist: Confirm the product category is currently eligible; Test against the active specification version; Complete third-party certification and registration; Report changes that affect qualified configuration
- Sources: Energy Star https://www.energystar.gov/
- Last verified: 2026-10-10

### ETSI EN 303 645 consumer IoT security baseline (EN 303 645)
- Page: https://hi-spark.net/certification/etsi-303-645.html
- Group: Security and privacy | Region: International baseline | Status: Voluntary baseline, referenced by regulation
- Issued or recognised by: ETSI, developed with industry and regulators
- Summary: Widely referenced baseline of thirteen security provisions for consumer IoT devices, from no universal default passwords to secure updates.
- Meaning: EN 303 645 is not a market access requirement by itself, but several national schemes and retailer requirements use it as the reference. Compliance is usually evidenced by a test report against the provisions plus the corresponding data protection guidance.
- Applies to: Consumer IoT devices such as cameras, hubs and sensors; Companion mobile apps and cloud services; Manufacturers designing a security baseline programme
- Does not cover: Industrial or medical device security requirements; Full ISO 27001 style management system certification; Legal data protection compliance
- Verification checklist: Eliminate universal default passwords and enforce unique credentials; Provide a vulnerability disclosure contact and process; Publish a support period and update policy; Secure sensitive data in transit and at rest; Test the device against the thirteen provisions
- Sources: ETSI consumer IoT security https://www.etsi.org/technologies/consumer-iot-security
- Last verified: 2026-10-10

### EN 18031 harmonised standards under the RED (EN 18031)
- Page: https://hi-spark.net/certification/en-18031.html
- Group: Security and privacy | Region: European Union | Status: Linked to EU market access
- Issued or recognised by: CEN/CENELEC standards, cited under the Radio Equipment Directive
- Summary: Harmonised standards that give a presumption of conformity with the cybersecurity requirements added to the Radio Equipment Directive.
- Meaning: With the delegated regulation applying from 1 August 2025, internet-connected radio equipment must meet network protection, personal data protection and fraud protection requirements. EN 18031-1, -2 and -3 are the main routes, and testing is done by notified bodies.
- Applies to: Internet-connected radio equipment in the EU; Wearables, cameras, toys and home devices with apps; Devices that process personal data or allow payments
- Does not cover: GDPR duties of the service operator; Radio performance and EMC testing; Security of back-end services outside the device scope
- Verification checklist: Confirm which of the three standards applies to the product; Map device features against each requirement clause; Engage a notified body early in the schedule; Keep the assessment in the technical file with the declaration of conformity
- Sources: EUR-Lex delegated regulation 2022/30 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg_del/2022/30/oj; ETSI consumer IoT security https://www.etsi.org/technologies/consumer-iot-security
- Last verified: 2026-10-10

### NIST IR 8259 IoT cybersecurity baseline (NIST 8259)
- Page: https://hi-spark.net/certification/nist-8259.html
- Group: Security and privacy | Region: United States framework | Status: Voluntary framework
- Issued or recognised by: National Institute of Standards and Technology
- Summary: A voluntary baseline of six foundational cybersecurity activities for connected devices, used widely in procurement and product planning.
- Meaning: NIST IR 8259 describes what a manufacturer should do before a device reaches the market, and 8259A lists the corresponding device capabilities. It is often used together with the IoT device cybersecurity guidance for federal acquisition.
- Applies to: Manufacturers planning device security features; Procurement requirements that reference NIST guidance; Products seeking a documented baseline for enterprise buyers
- Does not cover: A certification or a mark; Privacy law compliance; Sector-specific regulation such as medical devices
- Verification checklist: Identify the device and its security assumptions; Define the customer-facing security capabilities; Document the update and vulnerability handling model; Map the device against the six activities and 8259A capabilities
- Sources: NIST cybersecurity for IoT https://www.nist.gov/itl/applied-cybersecurity/nist-cybersecurity-iot-program; NIST IR 8259 https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/ir/8259/final
- Last verified: 2026-10-10

### US Cyber Trust Mark (US Cyber Trust Mark)
- Page: https://hi-spark.net/certification/cyber-trust-mark.html
- Group: Security and privacy | Region: United States | Status: Voluntary labelling programme
- Issued or recognised by: FCC with programme administrators
- Summary: A voluntary US labelling programme for consumer IoT cybersecurity, developed from the FCC cyber labelling initiative.
- Meaning: The label is intended to give shoppers a simple signal that a device meets a defined security baseline, including unique passwords, updates and vulnerability handling. Programme details and the list of recognised administrators continue to develop, so the current requirements should be confirmed before planning a launch around the mark.
- Applies to: Consumer IoT products sold in the United States; Retailers and marketplaces that promote the label; Manufacturers planning a security differentiation strategy
- Does not cover: Radio equipment authorisation, which is separate; A substitute for privacy law compliance; Industrial or enterprise device security
- Verification checklist: Check the current programme scope and requirements; Align the device with the underlying security criteria; Plan for third-party testing and label administration; Keep a public support and update commitment
- Sources: FCC Cyber Trust Mark https://www.fcc.gov/cybertrustmark
- Last verified: 2026-10-10

### IEC 62443 industrial cybersecurity (IEC 62443)
- Page: https://hi-spark.net/certification/iec-62443.html
- Group: Security and privacy | Region: International | Status: Voluntary, often contractual
- Issued or recognised by: International Electrotechnical Commission and ISA
- Summary: A family of standards for cybersecurity of industrial automation and control systems, covering processes, systems and components.
- Meaning: IEC 62443 is the reference for industrial IoT, gateways and building systems. Buyers often require a security level target such as SL 1 or SL 2, and evidence is usually produced through a certification or an independent assessment.
- Applies to: Industrial gateways, controllers and sensors; Building and energy management devices; Vendors selling into critical infrastructure
- Does not cover: Consumer IoT baselines, which are lighter weight; Classic IT security certification; Functional safety requirements
- Verification checklist: Define the target security level and zones for the product; Apply secure development and hardening requirements; Document threat model, access control and update process; Complete an independent assessment or certification
- Sources: ISA/IEC 62443 https://www.isa.org/standards-and-publications/isa-standards/isa-iec-62443-series-of-standards
- Last verified: 2026-10-10

### Information security management (ISO/IEC 27001) (ISO 27001)
- Page: https://hi-spark.net/certification/iso-27001.html
- Group: Security and privacy | Region: International | Status: Voluntary, contractual
- Issued or recognised by: Accredited certification bodies
- Summary: Certification of a management system for information security, covering how an organisation protects its own and its customers’ data.
- Meaning: ISO/IEC 27001 certifies the organisation and its processes, not a specific device. For IoT companies it is most relevant to the cloud service, the mobile app backend and internal development practices, and it is frequently demanded in B2B procurement.
- Applies to: Cloud platforms and app backends; Companies operating customer data at scale; Vendors responding to enterprise security questionnaires
- Does not cover: Device level security requirements; Privacy law compliance, which ISO 27701 addresses; Product certification of any kind
- Verification checklist: Define the scope and statement of applicability; Assess risks and select controls; Operate the management system with evidence; Complete stage 1 and stage 2 audits and maintain surveillance audits
- Sources: ISO/IEC 27001 https://www.iso.org/standard/27001
- Last verified: 2026-10-10

### Privacy information management (ISO/IEC 27701) (ISO 27701)
- Page: https://hi-spark.net/certification/iso-27701.html
- Group: Security and privacy | Region: International | Status: Voluntary, contractual
- Issued or recognised by: Accredited certification bodies
- Summary: An extension to ISO/IEC 27001 and 27002 for privacy information management, covering controllers and processors of personal data.
- Meaning: ISO/IEC 27701 provides a management framework that maps to privacy regulation, which is useful for IoT companies handling location, camera or health data. It complements but does not replace legal compliance.
- Applies to: Cloud services that process personal data; Mobile apps collecting usage or account data; Organisations acting as data processors for enterprise clients
- Does not cover: A guarantee of legal compliance in each jurisdiction; Device level data protection requirements; Consumer consent management software
- Verification checklist: Start from an operational ISO/IEC 27001 management system; Identify the controller and processor roles; Extend the risk assessment to personal data; Document records of processing and retention
- Sources: ISO/IEC 27701 https://www.iso.org/standard/71670
- Last verified: 2026-10-10

### SOC 2 trust services report (SOC 2)
- Page: https://hi-spark.net/certification/soc-2.html
- Group: Security and privacy | Region: United States, used globally | Status: Voluntary, contractual
- Issued or recognised by: Licensed CPA firms
- Summary: An independent attestation report on controls covering security and, optionally, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality and privacy.
- Meaning: SOC 2 is a report rather than a certificate. Enterprise customers typically ask for a Type 1 point-in-time report first and a Type 2 report covering a period of operation as the service matures.
- Applies to: Cloud services and IoT platforms serving business customers; Mobile backend and data processing environments; Vendors in enterprise procurement processes
- Does not cover: Device firmware security; Consumer privacy law compliance; A public certification mark
- Verification checklist: Choose the relevant trust services criteria; Document policies and control evidence; Complete a readiness assessment before the audit; Publish the report under NDA to customers
- Sources: AICPA assurance services https://www.aicpa-cima.com/topic/audit-assurance
- Last verified: 2026-10-10

### EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR)
- Page: https://hi-spark.net/certification/gdpr.html
- Group: Security and privacy | Region: European Union | Status: Mandatory
- Issued or recognised by: EU data protection authorities
- Summary: The core EU law on processing personal data, including data collected by connected devices, apps and cloud services.
- Meaning: IoT products routinely process personal data such as account details, device identifiers, location, camera footage or health measurements. GDPR requires a lawful basis, transparency, data minimisation, security, retention limits and support for data subject rights, and it applies to sellers outside the EU that target EU users.
- Applies to: Companion apps and cloud accounts; Cameras, trackers and wearables that process personal data; Manufacturers and service providers offering devices to EU users
- Does not cover: Radio or safety market access; Sector rules such as the ePrivacy Directive for cookies and communications; Local implementation laws that add national requirements
- Verification checklist: Map what personal data each product collects and where it goes; Define the lawful basis and document it; Publish a privacy notice that matches the actual data flows; Implement retention, deletion and export capabilities; Assess transfers outside the EU and the safeguards used
- Sources: EU data protection https://commission.europa.eu/law/law-topic/data-protection_en
- Last verified: 2026-10-10

### California consumer privacy rights (CCPA / CPRA)
- Page: https://hi-spark.net/certification/ccpa-cpra.html
- Group: Security and privacy | Region: California, United States | Status: Mandatory in scope
- Issued or recognised by: California Privacy Protection Agency and the Attorney General
- Summary: California privacy law giving consumers rights over personal information, including the right to know, delete, correct and opt out of sale or sharing.
- Meaning: Businesses meeting the thresholds must provide notices at collection, honour consumer requests and manage contracts with service providers. Device identifiers and precise location data count as personal information, so companion apps and cloud services are usually in scope.
- Applies to: Businesses serving California residents; Companion apps and cloud services; Ad tech and analytics integrations
- Does not cover: EU data protection rules; Sector rules such as health data laws; Device level security requirements
- Verification checklist: Confirm whether the business thresholds apply; Update the privacy notice and collection disclosures; Implement request handling and identity verification; Review contracts with analytics and advertising partners
- Sources: California CCPA https://oag.ca.gov/privacy/ccpa; California Privacy Protection Agency https://cppa.ca.gov/
- Last verified: 2026-10-10

### Children’s online privacy (COPPA) (COPPA)
- Page: https://hi-spark.net/certification/coppa.html
- Group: Security and privacy | Region: United States | Status: Mandatory in scope
- Issued or recognised by: Federal Trade Commission
- Summary: US rule that restricts collecting personal information from children under thirteen without verifiable parental consent.
- Meaning: Smart toys, kids’ watches and children’s cameras are a direct COPPA risk area because they combine cameras, microphones, location and app accounts. The rule also constrains third-party analytics and advertising in child-directed services.
- Applies to: Smart toys, kids’ watches and children’s trackers; Apps and services directed to children; Sites with actual knowledge of child users
- Does not cover: Radio and safety approvals; EU child data rules such as GDPR Article 8; School procurement rules
- Verification checklist: Decide whether the product or app is child-directed; Minimise collection and disable behavioural advertising where required; Implement verifiable parental consent where needed; Provide parental review and deletion routes; Review vendor data flows for child data
- Sources: FTC COPPA rule https://www.ftc.gov/legal-library/browse/rules/childrens-online-privacy-protection-rule-coppa
- Last verified: 2026-10-10

### Wi-Fi Alliance certification (Wi-Fi CERTIFIED)
- Page: https://hi-spark.net/certification/wi-fi-certified.html
- Group: Interoperability | Region: International | Status: Voluntary, widely required
- Issued or recognised by: Wi-Fi Alliance
- Summary: Certification programme that confirms a product interoperates with Wi-Fi networks and supports the security and feature set claimed on the package.
- Meaning: Certification covers the tested configuration, including the chipset, firmware and antenna design. Wi-Fi 6, Wi-Fi 6E, Wi-Fi 7, WPA3 and EasyMesh are separate programmes, and a device can carry more than one designation.
- Applies to: Access points, routers, extenders and mesh systems; Cameras, doorbells and appliances with Wi-Fi; Modules used as part of a certified end product
- Does not cover: Radio regulatory approval such as FCC or CE; Internet service quality or cloud performance; Mesh performance in every building layout
- Verification checklist: Choose the certifications that match the marketing claims; Test at an authorised laboratory using the correct test plan; Transfer the module certification conditions to the host design; Display the certification marks and identifiers correctly
- Sources: Wi-Fi Alliance certification https://www.wi-fi.org/certification
- Last verified: 2026-10-10

### Bluetooth qualification (Bluetooth SIG)
- Page: https://hi-spark.net/certification/bluetooth-sig.html
- Group: Interoperability | Region: International | Status: Required to use Bluetooth marks
- Issued or recognised by: Bluetooth Special Interest Group
- Summary: Membership, declaration and qualification process that lets a product use the Bluetooth trademarks and claim version support.
- Meaning: Products must be qualified through the Bluetooth SIG and listed, and the design must be declared by the member company. Component declarations from a module supplier can reduce the test scope but not the obligation to declare the final product.
- Applies to: Accessories, wearables and audio devices; Devices using Bluetooth Low Energy for setup or sensors; Modules embedded in a larger product
- Does not cover: Radio approval in the destination countries; Wi-Fi or cellular certification; App store requirements
- Verification checklist: Join the Bluetooth SIG as a member; Use qualified components and record their declarations; Complete the declaration and product listing; Keep the qualified design version aligned with shipped firmware
- Sources: Bluetooth qualification https://www.bluetooth.com/develop-with-bluetooth/qualification-listing/
- Last verified: 2026-10-10

### Matter certification (Matter)
- Page: https://hi-spark.net/certification/matter.html
- Group: Interoperability | Region: International | Status: Voluntary, ecosystem dependent
- Issued or recognised by: Connectivity Standards Alliance (CSA)
- Summary: Application-layer standard that lets smart home devices work across Apple Home, Google Home, Amazon Alexa and SmartThings.
- Meaning: Matter certification requires a CSA membership, test event participation and certification by an authorised test provider. Products are certified by device type, and the ecosystem still controls which features are exposed in each app.
- Applies to: Lights, plugs, sensors, locks and bridges; Hubs and border routers that commission Matter devices; Brands that want multi-ecosystem support
- Does not cover: Every feature of the manufacturer app; Cloud-to-cloud integrations that are not part of Matter; Radio approval
- Verification checklist: Register as a CSA member and obtain a vendor ID; Implement the correct device type and clusters; Pass the test harness and complete certification; Submit the product to the ecosystem programmes you support
- Sources: CSA Matter https://csa-iot.org/all-solutions/matter/
- Last verified: 2026-10-10

### Thread certification (Thread)
- Page: https://hi-spark.net/certification/thread.html
- Group: Interoperability | Region: International | Status: Voluntary, ecosystem dependent
- Issued or recognised by: Thread Group
- Summary: Certification for Thread mesh networking, the low-power IP transport commonly used with Matter devices.
- Meaning: Thread certification is separate from Matter certification, and many products need both. Border routers have additional requirements, and the network relies on a Thread border router to reach the internet.
- Applies to: Low-power sensors, locks and lighting; Border routers and hubs; Matter over Thread devices
- Does not cover: Matter application layer certification; Wi-Fi or Bluetooth function; Radio approval
- Verification checklist: Join the Thread Group and use qualified components; Test against the current Thread specification version; Certify the border router separately where applicable; Validate coexistence with Wi-Fi in the target band
- Sources: Thread Group https://www.threadgroup.org/
- Last verified: 2026-10-10

### Zigbee certification (Zigbee)
- Page: https://hi-spark.net/certification/zigbee.html
- Group: Interoperability | Region: International | Status: Voluntary, ecosystem dependent
- Issued or recognised by: Connectivity Standards Alliance (CSA)
- Summary: Certification for Zigbee devices and the Zigbee Certified programme, including Zigbee 3.0 device types.
- Meaning: Zigbee remains the most widely deployed low-power mesh in hubs and sensors. Certification confirms the device interoperates at the application layer with certified devices, while vendor-specific clusters can still limit cross-brand features.
- Applies to: Sensors, plugs, switches and lighting; Zigbee coordinators sold inside hubs; Devices intended for multi-brand zigbee networks
- Does not cover: Matter certification; Wi-Fi performance; Cloud features of the vendor app
- Verification checklist: Implement the correct Zigbee device type and clusters; Validate against certified devices from other vendors; Complete CSA certification testing; Document vendor-specific behaviour for support teams
- Sources: CSA Zigbee https://csa-iot.org/all-solutions/zigbee/
- Last verified: 2026-10-10

### Qi wireless charging certification (Qi)
- Page: https://hi-spark.net/certification/qi-wpc.html
- Group: Interoperability | Region: International | Status: Voluntary, widely adopted
- Issued or recognised by: Wireless Power Consortium
- Summary: Certification for inductive wireless charging products under the Qi standard, covering transmitters and receivers.
- Meaning: Qi certification verifies power transfer and safety behaviour between a transmitter and receiver, including foreign object detection. Products that claim Qi compatibility should be certified rather than only tested in-house.
- Applies to: Wireless charging pads and stands; Wearables and phones with wireless charging; Accessories sold as Qi compatible
- Does not cover: Wired charging safety; Battery certification; Radio approval for any wireless data function
- Verification checklist: Confirm the Qi power profile and coil design; Test transmitter and receiver as a pair; Complete WPC certification and listing; Apply the Qi logo under the licence terms
- Sources: Wireless Power Consortium https://www.wirelesspowerconsortium.com/
- Last verified: 2026-10-10

- Limitations: Feature availability varies by Ring model; Live view and announcements may require compatible Echo displays or speakers; Account and region restrictions can apply
- Steps: Open the Alexa app; Enable the Ring skill; Link the Ring account; Discover devices; Assign devices to rooms; Test voice commands and notifications

## Troubleshooting guides (40)

### Camera will not connect to Wi-Fi
- Page: https://hi-spark.net/troubleshooting/camera-will-not-connect-to-wifi.html
- Category: Security Cameras
- Symptom: A security camera cannot join the local Wi-Fi network or repeatedly drops offline.
- Likely causes: 2.4 GHz-only camera paired to a 5 GHz network; Weak signal at the installation point; Wrong Wi-Fi password or security mode; Router isolation or guest network restrictions; Camera already paired to another account
- Quick checks: Confirm the camera supports 2.4 GHz and/or 5 GHz; Move the camera near the router for setup; Confirm the password and SSID; Disable client isolation during setup; Remove the old device entry from the app if needed
- Steps: Factory reset the camera using the official procedure; Connect the phone to the intended 2.4 GHz network; Open the official app and start a fresh pairing; Enter the correct Wi-Fi credentials; Wait for the pairing confirmation before moving the camera; Test live view at the final installation point
- Escalate when: If the camera connects near the router but fails outside, improve Wi-Fi coverage with a mesh node or access point rather than repeatedly resetting the camera.
- Last verified: 2026-10-10

### Matter device will not pair
- Page: https://hi-spark.net/troubleshooting/matter-device-will-not-pair.html
- Category: Matter
- Symptom: The Matter setup code fails, the device is not discovered or pairing stops before completion.
- Likely causes: Device is not in pairing mode; Phone is on the wrong Wi-Fi or Thread network; Thread border router unavailable; Old controller firmware; Setup code already used or device still paired elsewhere
- Quick checks: Confirm the device is Matter-certified; Check whether the device uses Wi-Fi or Thread; Update the controller and device firmware; Confirm Bluetooth is enabled during commissioning; Remove stale pairings from other ecosystems
- Steps: Reset the Matter device using the manufacturer procedure; Open the intended controller app; Scan the Matter QR code or enter the manual pairing code; Keep the phone near the device during commissioning; Complete naming and room assignment; Test local control before adding a second controller
- Escalate when: For Thread devices, verify that a compatible Thread border router is online and that IPv6 is enabled on the network.
- Last verified: 2026-10-10

### Zigbee device keeps going offline
- Page: https://hi-spark.net/troubleshooting/zigbee-device-offline.html
- Category: Zigbee
- Symptom: A Zigbee sensor, light or lock shows offline or responds slowly in the app.
- Likely causes: Weak mesh coverage; Hub or coordinator overloaded; Wi-Fi and Zigbee channel interference; Battery or power issue; Device dropped from the mesh
- Quick checks: Check battery and power; Confirm the hub is online; Review Zigbee channel and Wi-Fi channel overlap; Check how many routers are in the Zigbee mesh; Test the device near the hub
- Steps: Bring the device near the hub and test; Re-pair it if it remains offline; Add a mains-powered Zigbee router device between hub and sensor; Move the hub away from the router and USB 3 devices; Rebuild or refresh the mesh if the platform supports it
- Escalate when: If only one room fails, treat it as a coverage problem first. If all devices fail, troubleshoot the hub, coordinator and channel plan.
- Last verified: 2026-10-10

### Smart Life cannot find a device
- Page: https://hi-spark.net/troubleshooting/smart-life-device-not-found.html
- Category: Smart Home
- Symptom: A Tuya or Smart Life device is not discovered during pairing.
- Likely causes: Device is in a different pairing mode; Bluetooth or location permission is blocked; Device is paired to another account; App region or data center mismatch; Unsupported Wi-Fi band during commissioning
- Quick checks: Confirm the correct app and account region; Enable Bluetooth and local network permissions; Place the device near the phone; Reset the device to pairing mode; Check whether it is already paired to another account
- Steps: Remove any previous device entry; Reset the device according to the manufacturer manual; Open the matching app and choose Add Device; Select auto-discovery or the correct category; Complete Wi-Fi credentials and wait for the device to register; Rename the device and test control
- Escalate when: If the device uses a manufacturer-specific white-label app, do not assume Tuya Smart or Smart Life will control it. Verify the app stated in the official manual.
- Last verified: 2026-10-10

### Ring doorbell shows offline
- Page: https://hi-spark.net/troubleshooting/ring-doorbell-offline.html
- Category: Video Doorbells
- Symptom: The Ring doorbell appears offline or stops sending notifications.
- Likely causes: Weak Wi-Fi signal; Battery or power issue; Router or ISP outage; Ring service or account issue; Device needs restart
- Quick checks: Check battery or wired power; Test Wi-Fi at the door location; Check the Ring status page and home internet; Confirm the device is not in setup mode
- Steps: Open the Ring app and check device health; Restart the router if other devices are offline; Power-cycle the doorbell using the official procedure; Reconnect to Wi-Fi if credentials or network changed; Test motion alerts and live view
- Escalate when: If only the doorbell is offline, focus on door-side Wi-Fi coverage, transformer power or battery condition.
- Last verified: 2026-10-10

### Camera does not detect the microSD card
- Page: https://hi-spark.net/troubleshooting/sd-card-not-detected.html
- Category: Storage
- Symptom: The camera app reports no storage, format failure or unusable local recording.
- Likely causes: Card format is unsupported; Counterfeit or worn card; Card exceeds supported capacity; Firmware bug; Card inserted incorrectly
- Quick checks: Confirm the maximum supported capacity; Use a reputable card rated for continuous recording; Format the card in the camera or official app; Check the card on a computer; Update camera firmware
- Steps: Power off the camera; Remove and reinsert the card correctly; Let the camera or app format the card; Test recording locally; Replace the card if format or write operations still fail
- Escalate when: Continuous-recording cameras require high-endurance cards. A card that works in a phone may still fail in a camera.
- Last verified: 2026-10-10

### Smart lock calibration failed
- Page: https://hi-spark.net/troubleshooting/smart-lock-calibration-failed.html
- Category: Smart Locks
- Symptom: The lock app reports calibration failure, incorrect lock state or incomplete bolt travel.
- Likely causes: Door alignment or strike plate friction; Bolt not moving freely; Adapter or mounting issue; Battery level too low; Firmware or app calibration state
- Quick checks: Check manual bolt movement; Inspect door alignment and strike plate; Replace batteries; Confirm the correct adapter and installation; Update firmware
- Steps: Calibrate with the door open; Check whether the bolt moves freely by hand; Adjust the strike plate or door alignment; Run calibration again; Test lock and unlock several times; Reinstall the app device entry only if calibration remains corrupted
- Escalate when: Do not force the motor. Friction in the door frame is a mechanical problem that software calibration cannot solve.
- Last verified: 2026-10-10

### IoT certificate rotation failed
- Page: https://hi-spark.net/troubleshooting/iot-certificate-rotation.html
- Category: Cloud IoT
- Symptom: A device fleet cannot reconnect after a certificate expires or a rotation policy changes.
- Likely causes: Expired device certificate; Wrong CA chain; Clock skew on the device; Policy or thing registration mismatch; OTA rotation job failed
- Quick checks: Check certificate validity dates; Confirm the device clock; Validate the CA chain; Compare device identity and policy in the cloud console; Test one pilot device before fleet rollout
- Steps: Identify the affected certificate and device group; Issue the replacement certificate; Test mutual TLS from one pilot device; Deploy rotation through a controlled OTA job; Monitor reconnect and error rates; Revoke the old certificate after the rollout
- Escalate when: Always keep a documented rollback path. Never rotate the entire fleet before validating DNS, time sync, TLS and the provisioning workflow.
- Last verified: 2026-10-10

### Robot vacuum cannot find its dock
- Page: https://hi-spark.net/troubleshooting/robot-vacuum-cannot-find-dock.html
- Category: Robot Vacuums
- Symptom: The robot cleans but cannot return to the charging dock, or it reports that it is lost.
- Likely causes: Dock moved after the map was saved; Dock power cable or adapter unplugged; Dock placed with obstructed approach or on a dark surface; Lidar or camera sensor covered with dust; Saved map out of date after furniture changed
- Quick checks: Check that the dock light is on; Confirm the dock is on a hard, level surface with clear space in front; Wipe the sensors and charging contacts; Check the app for a lost or incomplete map
- Steps: Return the robot to the dock by hand and confirm it charges; Clean the dock contacts and the robot charging pads; In the app, delete and rebuild the map; Re-add no-go zones and room names; Run a short clean and watch the return-to-dock behaviour; Only then move the dock if placement is still wrong
- Escalate when: If the robot finds the dock from the app but not when it finishes a run, the saved map is usually stale: delete the map, relearn and re-add the no-go zones rather than moving the dock again.
- Last verified: 2026-10-14

### Smart plug shows online but does not switch
- Page: https://hi-spark.net/troubleshooting/smart-plug-online-but-not-switching.html
- Category: Smart Home
- Symptom: The plug reports online in the app, but toggling it does nothing or the relay clicks and returns to the previous state.
- Likely causes: Firmware update in progress or failed; Local safety limit or power threshold triggered; Relay has reached end of life after heavy switching; Automation or schedule overriding manual control; Cloud or account state out of sync with the device
- Quick checks: Try the physical button on the plug; Check the app for a firmware update prompt or error; Disable schedules and automations for that plug; Confirm the plug is not reporting over-temperature or over-power
- Steps: Press the physical button to test basic switching; Remove any schedule or scene for the plug; Update firmware and wait for the reboot; Power-cycle the plug at the socket for ten seconds; Re-test switching from the app; If the relay still does not hold, replace the plug
- Escalate when: If the plug is warm, buzzes or trips a breaker, stop using it and replace it. Switching faults on mains hardware are a safety issue, not a software one.
- Last verified: 2026-10-14

### Video doorbell sends no motion alerts
- Page: https://hi-spark.net/troubleshooting/doorbell-no-motion-alerts.html
- Category: Video Doorbells
- Symptom: Live view works but motion notifications never arrive on the phone.
- Likely causes: Notification permission disabled for the app; Sensitivity or motion zones set so the area is excluded; Phone battery optimisation stopping background alerts; Subscription feature expired or not enabled; Firmware bug after an update
- Quick checks: Check the phone notification settings for the app; Open motion zones and sensitivity in the app; Confirm the doorbell is online in the app; Check whether alerts arrive with the app open
- Steps: Review motion zones, sensitivity and alert schedule; Enable background refresh and disable battery optimisation for the app; Update the doorbell and app firmware; Test in front of the doorbell with the app closed; If alerts never fire, reset the device and re-add it to the account
- Escalate when: If alerts arrive while the app is open but never in the background, the phone is killing the app: check battery optimisation and background refresh for the app rather than reinstalling the doorbell.

### The app cannot find a device because of the account region
- Page: https://hi-spark.net/troubleshooting/app-account-region-mismatch.html
- Category: Smart Home
- Symptom: After moving, changing Wi-Fi or reinstalling the app, a device that used to work is invisible during pairing.
- Likely causes: App account is registered in a different region than the device; Data centre selection changed during app installation; Device is still claimed by another account; Device was bought in a region whose server differs from the phone account
- Quick checks: Check the account region in the app settings; Compare the app data centre with the country where you bought the device; Confirm the device appears offline rather than missing in the old account; Check whether the device is still bound to a previous owner
- Steps: Open the app settings and read the account region; If needed, register a second account in the device region; Remove the device from the old account first; Reset and pair the device on the matching region account; Document which account owns which device to avoid repeating this
- Escalate when: Do not factory-reset the device before checking the region: a factory reset on a device bound to another region usually makes the problem worse and can delete local schedules.

### Streaming device or smart TV will not join Wi-Fi
- Page: https://hi-spark.net/troubleshooting/streaming-device-wont-join-wifi.html
- Category: TV and Streaming
- Symptom: A TV, stick or streaming device cannot see the network or fails at the password step.
- Likely causes: Device supports only 2.4 GHz while the network name exists on 5 GHz; WPA3-only or mixed security mode not supported by older firmware; Special characters in the password rejected by the device keyboard; MAC filtering or access control list on the router; Router band steering hiding the 2.4 GHz SSID
- Quick checks: Check the device specifications for the supported bands; Temporarily disable WPA3 or use WPA2/WPA3 mixed mode; Try the password on a phone keyboard to spot typing issues; Look for MAC filtering in the router settings
- Steps: Separate the 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz SSIDs on the router; Connect the device to the 2.4 GHz network; If it fails, set the router to WPA2-PSK for the test; Temporarily disable band steering and access control; After the device connects, restore security settings one at a time
- Escalate when: If the TV connects to a phone hotspot but never to the home router, suspect the router security mode or band steering rather than the TV.

- Page: https://hi-spark.net/troubleshooting/thread-device-offline-border-router.html
- Category: Thread
- Symptom: Matter-over-Thread sensors and lights stop responding but their battery and app status look normal.

- Quick checks: Check that the border router is powered and online; Confirm the hub shows in the app as a Thread border router; Check whether other Thread devices respond; Look for a recent router or ISP change affecting IPv6

- Escalate when: Thread devices depend on a working border router and IPv6. If every Thread device fails at once, troubleshoot the border router and the network before touching individual devices.

### Bluetooth device will not pair with the phone
- Page: https://hi-spark.net/troubleshooting/ble-device-wont-pair-with-phone.html

- Symptom: A wearable, lock or sensor in pairing mode never appears in the app or in the phone Bluetooth list.

### Firmware update stalls at a percentage
- Page: https://hi-spark.net/troubleshooting/firmware-update-stuck.html
- Category: Firmware
- Symptom: An over-the-air update sits at the same percentage for a long time, fails, or the device becomes unresponsive afterwards.
- Likely causes: Unstable Wi-Fi or low signal during download; Battery below the required level for the update; Interrupted by a reboot, power cut or app being closed; Update server or CDN issue; Device storage or partition too full for the image

- Escalate when: Never power off a device mid-update on purpose. If it is unresponsive after twenty minutes, follow the vendor recovery procedure rather than repeatedly cutting power.

### Camera night vision is washed out or stays in black and white
- Page: https://hi-spark.net/troubleshooting/camera-night-vision-problem.html
- Category: Security Cameras
- Symptom: At night the image looks washed out, shows a bright ring, or the camera never switches to infrared.
- Likely causes: Camera mounted behind a window causing IR reflection; IR LEDs disabled in the app or on a schedule; Dust, cobwebs or water on the lens or IR ring; Nearby light source defeating the day/night threshold; Hardware fault in the IR cut filter after long use
- Quick checks: Check the night vision setting in the app; Clean the lens and the ring of IR LEDs; Look for a bright spot or halo in the image; Test with the room in complete darkness
- Steps: Clean the lens and IR ring with a dry microfibre cloth; Set night vision to auto in the app; Remove the camera from behind glass if a halo appears; Adjust nearby lights so the camera is not fooled into day mode; If the image stays colour in darkness, the IR cut filter is likely faulty

### Smart lock battery drains in days
- Page: https://hi-spark.net/troubleshooting/smart-lock-battery-drains-fast.html
- Category: Smart Locks
- Symptom: A battery-powered smart lock reports low battery far sooner than the expected months of use.
- Likely causes: Motor straining against a misaligned strike plate; Wrong battery chemistry or brand (alkaline vs lithium requirements); Wi-Fi or Matter polling more often than the lock supports; Frequent auto-unlock or geofence triggers; Firmware bug or repeated pairing attempts
- Quick checks: Check whether the bolt moves freely by hand; Confirm the battery type in the official manual; Review auto-unlock and geofence settings; Look for repeated reconnect or pairing events in the app
- Steps: Lubricate and align the bolt, strike plate and frame; Fit the exact battery type the manual requires; Disable auto-unlock and geofence rules temporarily; Re-seat the lock in the app or reset it once; Monitor drain for one week with the new settings; If drain continues, escalate to the manufacturer
- Escalate when: If the lock is warm around the battery compartment or the drain continues with a fresh set of the recommended cells, stop using it and contact the manufacturer: internal drain on mains-free hardware is a safety matter.

### Camera live view lags or keeps buffering
- Page: https://hi-spark.net/troubleshooting/wifi-camera-live-view-lag.html
- Category: Security Cameras
- Symptom: Live view opens but stutters, drops frames or takes many seconds to start.
- Likely causes: Weak Wi-Fi signal at the camera; Upload bandwidth saturated by other devices; Streaming the main high-bitrate stream instead of the substream; Camera overheating in direct sun; Cloud relay or account region adding latency
- Quick checks: Check reported Wi-Fi signal strength in the app; Try the lower-resolution stream; Test live view with other devices idle; Compare app performance on mobile data

- Page: https://hi-spark.net/troubleshooting/zigbee-pairing-fails.html
- Category: Zigbee
- Symptom: A Zigbee sensor or light never joins the hub, or it joins and immediately drops.

### Hub forgets devices after a power cut
- Page: https://hi-spark.net/troubleshooting/hub-loses-devices-after-power-cut.html
- Category: Smart Home Hubs
- Symptom: After an outage the hub comes back but several devices show offline or missing.
- Likely causes: Hub rebooted faster than the devices re-joined the mesh; Devices with weak batteries failed to rejoin; Network name or IP change after the outage; Corrupted local database after an unclean shutdown; Router took longer than the hub to come online
- Quick checks: Wait ten minutes and refresh the app before reacting; Check whether the hub is online in the app; Confirm the router and internet came back first; Look for devices that also lost battery level readings
- Steps: Reboot the router first, then the hub; Wait for the mesh to re-form and refresh the app; Re-add only the devices that stay offline; Update hub firmware; Add a small UPS for the hub and router to avoid unclean shutdowns
- Escalate when: If devices disappear after every outage, protect the hub with a small UPS or check the hub power supply rather than re-adding devices each time.

### Camera motion alerts fire constantly
- Page: https://hi-spark.net/troubleshooting/camera-motion-detection-too-sensitive.html
- Category: Security Cameras
- Symptom: Motion notifications trigger on swaying trees, headlights or rain instead of real events.
- Likely causes: Detection zones covering roads, trees or reflections; Sensitivity left at maximum; PIR sensor aimed at a heat source or moving shadow; Notification schedule disabled so alerts fire all day; Person detection not enabled where available

- Page: https://hi-spark.net/troubleshooting/smart-bulb-flickers.html
- Category: Lighting
- Symptom: An LED smart bulb flickers, buzzes or glows faintly when switched off.

- Page: https://hi-spark.net/troubleshooting/camera-sd-card-fills-quickly.html
- Category: Storage
- Symptom: Local storage wraps or stops recording much sooner than expected.
- Likely causes: Continuous recording enabled instead of events; High bitrate or high resolution profile; Too many false motion events triggering clips; Card capacity small for the recording profile; Card wearing out and remounting repeatedly
- Quick checks: Check whether recording mode is continuous or event-based; Review resolution and bitrate settings; Look at how many events are recorded per day; Check card health and capacity

- Page: https://hi-spark.net/troubleshooting/smart-plug-turns-off-randomly.html
- Category: Electrical
- Symptom: A plug or switch cuts power at random times without a scheduled action.
- Likely causes: Overload protection tripping under heavy load; Automation, timer or power threshold rule still active; Firmware restart after a failed update; Loose wiring in the plug or socket; Cloud outage leaving the device in a safe state
- Quick checks: Note the load connected when it switches off; Check the plug temperature; Review all scenes, timers and power rules; Check firmware version and recent restarts
