### Wi-Fi slows down with many smart devices
- Page: https://hi-spark.net/troubleshooting/wifi-router-too-many-devices.html
- Category: Networking
- Symptom: Smart plugs and cameras drop offline as more devices are added, and phones slow down in the same rooms.
- Likely causes: Client limit reached on the router or band; 2.4 GHz band congested with small devices; Single access point covering too large an area; DHCP pool too small for the number of devices; Cheap devices holding connections open
- Quick checks: Count connected devices in the router interface; Check which band each device uses; Look for DHCP address exhaustion messages; Test whether drops correlate with adding devices
- Steps: Raise the DHCP pool or shorten lease times; Move IoT devices to the 2.4 GHz band or a guest network; Add an access point or mesh node; Update router and device firmware; Replace devices that repeatedly rejoin the network
- Escalate when: If the router has reached its client limit, device tweaking will not help: add an access point or a dedicated IoT network instead of resetting devices.

### Solar panel does not keep the camera charged
- Page: https://hi-spark.net/troubleshooting/camera-solar-panel-not-charging.html
- Category: Power
- Symptom: A solar-powered camera keeps losing charge even on sunny days.
- Likely causes: Panel in shade or at the wrong angle for the season; Dirty or snow-covered panel; Cable or connector corroded or loose; Low winter sun plus heavy event traffic; Panel undersized for the camera power draw
- Quick checks: Check panel orientation and shading through the day; Clean the panel; Inspect the cable and connector; Review daily power consumption
- Steps: Reposition and tilt the panel towards the midday sun; Clean the panel and check cable and connector; Reduce event traffic and live view use; Update firmware and read the charge log; Measure panel output if the battery still drops, then replace the faulty part
- Escalate when: If a multimeter shows panel output but the camera never charges, the charging circuit or cable is faulty rather than the panel.
- Last verified: 2026-10-14

### GPS tracker reports the wrong location
- Page: https://hi-spark.net/troubleshooting/gps-tracker-location-inaccurate.html
- Category: Tracking
- Symptom: A tracker shows a location hundreds of metres off, jumps between places or stops updating.
- Likely causes: Indoor use where GPS is blocked; Assisted positioning using Wi-Fi or cell towers; Low battery forcing less frequent fixes; Poor sky view in cities or under cover; Firmware or platform mapping delay
- Quick checks: Compare the reported accuracy value in the app; Check whether the device reports LTE, Wi-Fi or GPS fixes; Test outdoors with a clear sky view; Note the update interval setting
- Steps: Force a manual location update outdoors; Check the reported positioning method and accuracy; Adjust the update interval and battery mode; Update firmware; If the device never gets a GPS fix outdoors, request a service check
- Escalate when: If the tracker is accurate outdoors but drifts indoors, the position comes from Wi-Fi or cell positioning rather than GPS: judge accuracy by the reported method.
- Last verified: 2026-10-14

- Verdict: LiDAR maps faster and works in the dark. Camera/vSLAM recognises objects better and is quieter with no turret.
- Best for: a: Large, cluttered floors mapped quickly, day or night.; b: Homes needing obstacle recognition of cables and pet waste.
- Editorial scores: LiDAR navigation 77, Camera (vSLAM) navigation 72 (editorial estimates, not a rating or valuation)
- Decision factors: 5

### Solar vs battery cameras
- Page: https://hi-spark.net/compare/solar-vs-battery-cameras.html
- Compares: Solar camera vs Battery-only camera (Device)
- Summary: Continuous top-up versus periodic charging.
- Verdict: Solar when the camera gets daylight and you want to set and forget. Battery-only in shade or for occasional use.
- Best for: a: Sunny outdoor positions that can stay mounted year-round.; b: Shaded walls and seasonal or temporary installs.
- Editorial scores: Solar camera 61, Battery-only camera 77 (editorial estimates, not a rating or valuation)
- Decision factors: 5

### Subscription vs one-time purchase
- Page: https://hi-spark.net/compare/subscription-vs-one-time.html
- Compares: Subscription model vs One-time purchase (Pricing)
- Summary: The single most under-estimated IoT buying decision.
- Verdict: Subscriptions buy convenience and off-site storage. One-time purchases lower lifetime cost and remove cloud dependency.
- Best for: a: Users who want remote access, AI alerts and no hardware maintenance.; b: Users who want predictable lifetime cost and local ownership.
- Editorial scores: Subscription model 61, One-time purchase 79 (editorial estimates, not a rating or valuation)
- Decision factors: 5

### Free vs paid camera cloud plans
- Page: https://hi-spark.net/compare/free-vs-paid-cloud-plans.html
- Compares: Free tier vs Paid tier (Pricing)
- Summary: What you actually lose when you do not pay.
- Verdict: Free tiers work for short clips and one camera. Paid plans become worthwhile once you run three or more cameras.
- Best for: a: Single-camera homes and low-stakes monitoring.; b: Multi-camera homes needing longer retention and richer alerts.
- Editorial scores: Free tier 52, Paid tier 72 (editorial estimates, not a rating or valuation)
- Decision factors: 5

### GDPR-first vs US-first cloud
- Page: https://hi-spark.net/compare/gdpr-vs-us-first-cloud.html
- Compares: GDPR-first platform vs US-first platform (Privacy)
- Summary: Where the data lives decides which contract you can sign.
- Verdict: GDPR-first for EU customers and public-sector work. US-first when the ecosystem and tooling outweigh residency complexity.
- Best for: a: Businesses serving EU residents or handling special-category data.; b: Products aimed primarily at North America.
- Editorial scores: GDPR-first platform 84, US-first platform 78 (editorial estimates, not a rating or valuation)
- Decision factors: 5

### EU vs US data residency
- Page: https://hi-spark.net/compare/eu-vs-us-data-residency.html
- Compares: EU region vs US region (Privacy)
- Summary: Compliance, latency and cost all change with region choice.
- Verdict: EU regions for European users. US regions for North American users - latency and legal exposure both follow the data.
- Best for: a: European customers and EU-based operations.; b: North American customers and US-first go-to-market.
- Editorial scores: EU region 81, US region 74 (editorial estimates, not a rating or valuation)
- Decision factors: 5

## Core concepts (33)
- Device shadow - A cloud-side copy of a device's reported and desired state. Why it matters: Lets you read and control a device that is offline, and gives the backend a single place to reconcile state.
- Digital twin - A live model of a physical asset, its sensors and its behaviour. Why it matters: Used for simulation, predictive maintenance and remote diagnosis without touching the physical asset.
- Over-the-air update - Delivering firmware or configuration to devices remotely. Why it matters: The main way security fixes reach deployed hardware; a poor OTA path is the most common long-term fleet risk.
- Commissioning - The process of joining a device to a network and an account. Why it matters: Commissioning failures are the largest source of consumer support tickets and returns.
- Device attestation - Cryptographic proof that a device is genuine and running approved firmware. Why it matters: Blocks cloned devices and compromised firmware from joining a fleet or a Matter fabric.
- Secure boot - A boot chain where each stage verifies the signature of the next. Why it matters: Prevents persistent firmware tampering on physically accessible devices.
- MQTT QoS levels - QoS 0 delivers at most once, QoS 1 at least once and QoS 2 exactly once. Why it matters: Choosing the wrong level either loses telemetry or creates duplicate processing and extra cost.
- Last-gasp message - A final status message sent as a device loses power. Why it matters: Turns a silent outage into a diagnosable event, which matters for alarms and safety-adjacent devices.
- Edge computing - Processing data near the device instead of in a central cloud region. Why it matters: Cuts latency and bandwidth, keeps sensitive data local and lets the system keep working offline.
- Fleet management - The tooling and process for managing thousands of deployed devices. Why it matters: Without it, firmware versions, certificates and configuration drift become unmanageable within months.
- Telemetry vs command channel - Telemetry flows device to cloud, commands flow cloud to device. Why it matters: Separating them lets you apply different security, retention and rate-limit policies to each direction.
- Time-series data - Telemetry stored as timestamped samples rather than mutable rows. Why it matters: Drives retention cost, query performance and the ability to detect trends and anomalies.
- Device identity - A unique, verifiable credential per device. Why it matters: Shared or reused credentials mean one compromised device can impersonate the whole fleet.
- Local-first architecture - Automation that runs locally and treats the cloud as an enhancement. Why it matters: Keeps lights, locks and alarms working when broadband or the vendor cloud is unavailable.
- Interoperability bridge - A gateway that exposes one ecosystem's devices to another. Why it matters: Vendor locks and ecosystem battles rarely end in one protocol winning, so bridges stay necessary.
- Obsolescence management - Planning for the end of cloud services, firmware support and spare parts. Why it matters: Connected products can be bricked by a cloud shutdown even when the hardware still works.
- Data minimisation - Collecting only the data the product actually needs. Why it matters: Reduces breach exposure, retention cost and regulatory risk under GDPR and similar laws.
- Latency budget - The total time from an event to a user-visible response, split across every hop. Why it matters: Makes latency discussions concrete instead of arguing about which single component is slow.
- Link budget - The accounting of transmit power, gains, path loss and receiver sensitivity. Why it matters: Determines whether a radio link will actually work at the claimed range in a real building.
- Duty cycle - The proportion of time a radio may transmit, often set by regulation. Why it matters: Sub-GHz bands are duty-cycle limited, so it caps how often a device can report in Europe.
- Matter fabric - A set of Matter devices sharing one controller and trust domain. Why it matters: Explains why a device can be on one app but not another, and why multi-admin matters.
- Direct thermal vs thermal transfer - Direct thermal prints by heating the paper; thermal transfer melts ribbon onto the label. Why it matters: Explains why some labels fade to blank in sunlight and others last years.
- Label adhesive type - Acrylic, rubber and hot-melt adhesives behave very differently on cold, damp or oily surfaces. Why it matters: Adhesive failure is the most common reason a label falls off long before the print fades.
- Print resolution (DPI) - Dots per inch of the print head, which sets the smallest readable barcode and text. Why it matters: A 203 dpi head cannot print the same barcode density as a 300 dpi head, regardless of the app.
- Audio codec latency - The delay a codec adds between the source and the speaker. Why it matters: Matters for gaming and video, where lip-sync errors above roughly 100 ms become noticeable.
- Room correction - Measuring a room and adjusting output to compensate for speaker placement and surfaces. Why it matters: A cheap speaker with correction often beats an expensive one placed badly.
- Multiroom synchronisation - Keeping separate speakers aligned within a few milliseconds so audio does not echo between rooms. Why it matters: The single hardest part of multiroom audio, and the reason closed ecosystems still win.
- Islanding - A system's ability to keep supplying a backed-up circuit while the grid is down. Why it matters: Decides whether a battery keeps your lights on during an outage, or only shifts your bill.
- State of charge vs state of health - Charge is how full the battery is now; health is how much capacity it has left over its life. Why it matters: Two batteries at 100% charge can behave very differently if one has aged.
- OCPP and charger lock-in - Charging networks speak OCPP to chargers, which determines whether you can switch providers. Why it matters: A charger without OCPP support ties you to one network indefinitely.
- Zone-based irrigation - Splitting watering into independently controlled circuits. Why it matters: Without zones, a schedule must satisfy the thirstiest plant and wastes water on the rest.
- Map persistence - Whether a robot vacuum keeps its floor plan between runs or rebuilds it each time. Why it matters: Rebuilding costs battery and time, and is the usual reason cleaning takes longer than expected.
- Screen-free coding - Teaching programming logic with physical tiles or buttons rather than a screen. Why it matters: Often the right entry point for younger children, and a useful fallback when app support ends.


## Protocols and standards (61)
- Wi-Fi - High-bandwidth wireless networking for cameras, hubs, appliances and home devices. | https://hi-spark.net/protocol/wifi.html
- Bluetooth LE - Low-energy pairing and control for wearables, locks, sensors and configuration. | https://hi-spark.net/protocol/bluetooth-le.html
- Zigbee - Low-power mesh networking widely used in sensors, lighting, locks and smart-home hubs. | https://hi-spark.net/protocol/zigbee.html
- Thread - Low-power IPv6 mesh designed for Matter, smart-home devices and border routers. | https://hi-spark.net/protocol/thread.html
- Matter - Cross-ecosystem application layer for smart-home devices across Wi-Fi, Ethernet and Thread. | https://hi-spark.net/protocol/matter.html
- Z-Wave - Sub-GHz mesh ecosystem common in security, locks, lighting and hubs. | https://hi-spark.net/protocol/z-wave.html
- MQTT - Publish-subscribe messaging protocol designed for constrained devices and unreliable networks. | https://hi-spark.net/protocol/mqtt.html
- HTTPS & REST - Secure request-response APIs used by cloud platforms, mobile apps and device management tools. | https://hi-spark.net/protocol/https-rest.html
- CoAP - UDP-based protocol for constrained IoT devices and low-bandwidth networks. | https://hi-spark.net/protocol/coap.html
- AMQP - Message-oriented protocol used by enterprise IoT platforms and cloud integrations. | https://hi-spark.net/protocol/amqp.html
- LoRaWAN - Long-range, low-power wide-area networking for sensors, agriculture and utility metering. | https://hi-spark.net/protocol/lorawan.html
- NB-IoT - Narrowband cellular service for low-power, low-data sensors and meters. | https://hi-spark.net/protocol/nb-iot.html
- LTE-M - LTE-based low-power cellular connectivity with better mobility and latency than NB-IoT. | https://hi-spark.net/protocol/lte-m.html
- 4G LTE - Cellular broadband for cameras, routers, hotspots and remote sites. | https://hi-spark.net/protocol/4g-lte.html
- 5G - High-throughput, low-latency cellular connectivity for gateways, video and industrial deployments. | https://hi-spark.net/protocol/5g.html
- eSIM - Embedded, remotely provisioned SIM profile for cellular devices and global fleets. | https://hi-spark.net/protocol/esim.html
- GNSS - Satellite positioning using GPS, Galileo, GLONASS, BeiDou and related constellations. | https://hi-spark.net/protocol/gnss.html
- Ultra-Wideband - Centimetre-accurate ranging for secure access and precise indoor location. | https://hi-spark.net/protocol/uwb.html
- NFC - Very short-range tap, pairing and payment technology. | https://hi-spark.net/protocol/nfc.html
- RFID - Radio-frequency identification for inventory, access and asset identification. | https://hi-spark.net/protocol/rfid.html
- Modbus - Decades-old industrial protocol, still the default for PLCs, meters and inverters. | https://hi-spark.net/protocol/modbus.html
- OPC UA - Secure industrial communication standard for machines, PLCs and industrial software. | https://hi-spark.net/protocol/opcua.html
- RS-485 - Differential serial physical layer used by Modbus RTU, BACnet MS/TP and many sensors. | https://hi-spark.net/protocol/rs485.html
- Ethernet - Reliable wired networking for NVRs, gateways, industrial devices and fixed infrastructure. | https://hi-spark.net/protocol/ethernet.html
- PoE - Combines data and power on Ethernet cabling for cameras, access points and IoT endpoints. | https://hi-spark.net/protocol/poe.html
- Wi-Fi HaLow - Sub-GHz Wi-Fi standard for longer-range, lower-power IoT devices. | https://hi-spark.net/protocol/wi-fi-halow.html
- Wi-Fi 6E / 7 - Modern Wi-Fi generations with higher throughput, lower latency and 6 GHz support. | https://hi-spark.net/protocol/wi-fi-6e-7.html
- Bluetooth Mesh - Many-to-many BLE mesh aimed at commercial lighting and building control. | https://hi-spark.net/protocol/ble-mesh.html
- IPv6 - Modern internet addressing and routing foundation for scalable IoT networks. | https://hi-spark.net/protocol/ipv6.html
- Digital Twin - Virtual representation of a physical device, asset or process for monitoring and simulation. | https://hi-spark.net/protocol/digital-twin.html
- Matter over Wi-Fi - Matter application layer carried over Wi-Fi for mains-powered devices. | https://hi-spark.net/protocol/matter-over-wifi.html
- Thread 1.4 - Latest Thread release adding better border router management, Thread over Infrastructure and improved diagnostics. | https://hi-spark.net/protocol/thread-1-4.html
- Wi-SUN - IEEE 802.15.4g based field area network for large outdoor smart-city and utility meshes. | https://hi-spark.net/protocol/wi-sun.html
- Zigbee Green Power - Energy-harvesting profile that lets batteryless switches and sensors join a Zigbee network. | https://hi-spark.net/protocol/zigbee-green-power.html
- Bluetooth Channel Sounding - Precise distance measurement over BLE for secure access and asset tracking. | https://hi-spark.net/protocol/ble-channel-sounding.html
- 5G RedCap - Reduced-capability 5G for wearables, industrial sensors and cameras that do not need full eMBB. | https://hi-spark.net/protocol/5g-redcap.html
- Satellite NTN IoT - Direct-to-satellite connectivity for devices outside terrestrial coverage. | https://hi-spark.net/protocol/ntn-satellite-iot.html
- Sigfox / 0G - Ultra-narrowband, very low data rate network for simple telemetry. | https://hi-spark.net/protocol/sigfox-0g.html
- mioty - ETSI-standardised LPWAN using telegram splitting for high reliability in dense networks. | https://hi-spark.net/protocol/mioty.html
- Wireless M-Bus - European standard for wireless utility metering in the 868 MHz band. | https://hi-spark.net/protocol/wm-bus.html
- Z-Wave Long Range - Z-Wave LR removes repeater limits and extends range for large installations. | https://hi-spark.net/protocol/zwave-long-range.html
- CAN bus - Robust vehicle and machine bus, now paired with IoT gateways for telematics. | https://hi-spark.net/protocol/can-bus.html
- LoRa point-to-point - Raw LoRa modulation without LoRaWAN, used for simple private links. | https://hi-spark.net/protocol/lora-p2p.html
- KNX - Long-established building automation standard for lighting, HVAC and blinds. | https://hi-spark.net/protocol/knx.html
- DALI-2 - Digital addressable lighting interface with certified control gear and sensors. | https://hi-spark.net/protocol/dali-2.html
- Ethernet TSN - Time-Sensitive Networking adds determinism and time sync to standard Ethernet. | https://hi-spark.net/protocol/ethernet-tsn.html
- MQTT-SN - MQTT for Sensor Networks, adapted for very constrained devices and non-TCP links. | https://hi-spark.net/protocol/mqtt-sn.html
- AirPrint - Apple driverless printing over the local network. | https://hi-spark.net/protocol/airprint.html
- IPP - Internet Printing Protocol, the standard behind driverless and cloud printing. | https://hi-spark.net/protocol/ipp.html
- ESC/POS - Epson command set that became the de facto standard for receipt and label printers. | https://hi-spark.net/protocol/escpos.html
- ZPL - Zebra Programming Language used to compose barcode and RFID labels. | https://hi-spark.net/protocol/zpl.html
- Bluetooth A2DP - Profile that carries stereo audio to headphones and speakers. | https://hi-spark.net/protocol/bluetooth-a2dp.html
- Bluetooth LE Audio - Next-generation Bluetooth audio with LC3 codec, multi-stream and broadcast. | https://hi-spark.net/protocol/le-audio.html
- AirPlay 2 - Apple streaming protocol with multiroom synchronisation. | https://hi-spark.net/protocol/airplay-2.html
- Google Cast - Google streaming protocol for casting audio and video to devices. | https://hi-spark.net/protocol/google-cast.html
- Spotify Connect - Streams Spotify directly to a device without routing through the phone. | https://hi-spark.net/protocol/spotify-connect.html
- DLNA / UPnP - Discovery and streaming standard for sharing media on a local network. | https://hi-spark.net/protocol/dlna-upnp.html
- SunSpec Modbus - Standard register map that lets monitoring software read inverters and batteries across brands. | https://hi-spark.net/protocol/sunspec-modbus.html
- OCPP - Open Charge Point Protocol, the standard link between a charger and a charging network. | https://hi-spark.net/protocol/ocpp.html
- Matter bridge - A device that exposes non-Matter products to a Matter fabric. | https://hi-spark.net/protocol/matter-bridge.html
- Wi-Fi sensing - Using changes in Wi-Fi signal to detect motion or presence without a dedicated sensor. | https://hi-spark.net/protocol/wifi-sensing.html
